We hope to launch the Verification Age for video models: 50 scientists, 6 months, 100 rule-based verifiers, 300 new tasks, and a worked RL recipe. 

Coding models are advancing crazily thanks to the synthetic RL envs paradigms. Verification via codes or Lean gives models super-human math/coding intelligence like that in Astra and Fable. 

However, video models are still in the GPT-3 stage, where we just dump million hours video data into the model training and hope for magic.

In this work, 
1) we built 100 rule-based verifiers each paired with a synthetic data generators which give 10k+ diverse samples within the task domain 
2) we made additional 300 tasks generators, including classic games i.e. Snake, Gold Miner, Mario, to further scale training data distribution with million samples rendered ready available on HuggingFace 
3)  ~60 experiments to find a worked RL recipe for video model post-training 
4) comparison studies between image models, unified models, video models - which is the best model for visual thinking? 
5) failure modes of how VLM-as-Judge will not satisfy video models RL in long term
6) interpretability studies show all image models, unified models, video models emerged "Schrödinger Effect", CoS reasoning through diffusion steps
7) many more insights

A RAINDROP LANDS IN YOUR HOMETOWN. WHERE DOES IT GO NEXT?

It's called River Runner Global.

Pick a spot on the map and watch a virtual raindrop follow a simulated route downstream through real river systems.

Not just a line on a map. an animated journey along the water's path (River Runner).

Adrop in Nebraska can follow the Platte into the Missouri, then the Mississippi, all the way to the Gulf of Mexico (explore the map).

Suddenly that boring river you drive past feels a little less boring.

You open it to try one random spot. then you try your hometown. then the mountains from your last vacation. then somewhere on the other side of the planet.

Aand now you're emotionally invested in where a pretend raindrop ends up.

Sam Learner built the visualization, with Dave Blodgett, Kyle Onda and Ben Webb developing the backend.

Just a website that turns “where does this water go?” into something you can actually follow.

Open the map. Pick somewhere familiar. See where the water takes you.

Robots don’t just need better models. They need better hands.

I tried @axisrobotics today and ended up controlling a virtual robot arm from my browser. It sounds simple until you actually have to make the movement precise.

That made me realize the real problem with Physical AI: models need huge amounts of real-world movement data, and collecting that data is anything but easy.

What I found interesting is that each completed task gets scored and recorded on-chain.

So instead of another “click to earn” campaign, it actually feels like your actions are becoming useful training data.

Curious how far this can go.
Would you try teaching a robot through your browser?
